nameStory: The Sunken Rim-lichen gets its name from its distinctive apothecia (reproductive structures) that appear to sink below the surface of the lichen's body, creating tiny crater-like depressions. Unlike many rim lichens where the fruiting bodies sit proudly on top, this species keeps its reproductive parts tucked down low, as if they're hiding in little sunken bowls.
description: Sunken Rim-lichen is a crustose (crust-like) lichen that forms thin, grayish patches on rock surfaces. It grows as a tight, crusty coating that can be difficult to peel away from its rocky home. The lichen typically reaches only a few centimeters across, though multiple patches may merge to cover larger areas. Its most distinctive feature is the small, dark reproductive structures that appear sunken into the lichen's surface rather than raised above it.

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Look for small, dark circular spots that appear pressed down into the lichen's surface, creating tiny crater-like depressions rather than raised bumps

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms a thin, crusty coating that adheres tightly to rock surfaces and feels rough and gritty when touched gently with a fingernail

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Appears pale gray to whitish-gray when dry, becoming slightly darker and more vibrant when wet from rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Found exclusively on hard rock surfaces, particularly favoring exposed granite, quartzite, or similar acidic rocks in sunny locations

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: The surface feels slightly powdery or granular to the touch, with a somewhat chalky texture that may leave faint residue on your fingers

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches typically span 1-3 centimeters across, though they may appear larger when multiple colonies grow together

habitat: Sunken Rim-lichen grows on exposed rock faces and boulders in New England's mountains and rocky outcrops, particularly favoring acidic rocks like granite. Look for it on sunny, well-ventilated rock surfaces at higher elevations, especially in the White Mountains of New Hampshire and similar rocky terrain throughout the region. It thrives in areas with good air circulation and minimal competition from faster-growing plants.

seasonality.spring: The lichen becomes more vibrant as spring moisture awakens it from winter dormancy. Look for the characteristic sunken reproductive structures which may be more noticeable as the lichen darkens slightly with increased moisture.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer weather, the lichen appears at its palest gray-white color and may seem almost chalky. The sunken apothecia remain visible as dark spots, making this an excellent time for identification on sunny rock faces.
seasonality.fall: Fall rains refresh the lichen, causing it to darken and become more prominent against the rock surface. The contrast between the lichen body and sunken reproductive structures is often most pronounced during this season.
seasonality.winter: Snow and ice may temporarily obscure the lichen, but it remains active beneath winter weather. On clear winter days, look for it on south-facing rocks where snow melts first.

funFact: Despite being with us year-round for potentially decades or even centuries, Sunken Rim-lichen has been documented only three times by observers in all of New England, making it rarer to spot than many birds that visit our region for just a few weeks each year!
confusionNotes: Many other rim lichens look similar at first glance, but most have raised, button-like reproductive structures sitting on top of the lichen surface. Remember: if the dark spots look like they're popping up, it's probably not Sunken Rim-lichen – you want the ones that look like they've been pressed down with a tiny thumb.
contextualKnowledge: The Lecanora genus contains many species that are notoriously difficult to distinguish without microscopic examination or chemical testing, so even experienced naturalists may need to note 'Lecanora species' rather than attempting a specific identification in the field.
compareHints: Unlike Common Rim Lichen which has prominent raised apothecia, or Granite-speck Rim Lichen which tends to form more scattered, speckled patterns, Sunken Rim-lichen's defining characteristic is those distinctive crater-like depressions. While Mealy Rim-lichen has a more powdery, flour-like surface texture, Sunken Rim-lichen feels more gritty and granular to the touch.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pink-eyed White-rim stands out from its Lecanora relatives by its distinctive pink to reddish-brown apothecia with white rims - most other rim lichens in the genus have brown, black, or yellow reproductive discs.
Among the rim lichens in its genus, Mapledust Lichen stands out for its distinctly dusty, powdery surface texture.
Among its rim-lichen relatives, Mealy Rim-lichen is distinguished by its distinctly granular, powdery surface texture.
Among its rim lichen relatives, Bumpy Rim-lichen stands out for having the most prominently raised fruiting bodies - they truly stick up from the surface rather than sitting flush with it.
Unlike its rim lichen relatives that prefer rock or bark, Driftwood Rim-lichen is uniquely specialized for weathered wood substrates.

Frosted Rim-lichen stands out from its Lecanora relatives by maintaining a consistently pale, whitish color rather than the grayer tones of Common Rim Lichen or the more yellowish hues of some other species in the genus.
Unlike many of its rim lichen relatives that grow on tree bark or soil, Granite-speck Rim Lichen is almost exclusively rock-dwelling.
Beaded Rim-lichen differs from its many Lecanora relatives primarily through its distinctive beaded apothecia rims - most other rim lichens in the genus have smooth, clean rim edges.
Among its rim lichen relatives, Dusted White-Rim stands out for its distinctly powdery surface texture, while species like Common Rim Lichen tend to have smoother surfaces.
Among its rim lichen relatives, this species tends to prefer more acidic substrates compared to Common Rim Lichen, which grows on more neutral bark.
Unlike the more common Granite-speck Rim Lichen which has a smoother surface, Lecanora intricata has that distinctive granular texture.

**Uncertain comparison warning** Among its Lecanora relatives, Common Rim Lichen is distinguished by its preference for exposed rock (unlike bark-dwelling species like Mealy Rim-lichen) and its particularly well-defined raised rims around the apothecia.
Unlike its more common relatives like Common Rim Lichen which often grows on tree bark, rim lichen is strictly a rock specialist.
Unlike the Common Rim Lichen which has clearly separate, well-defined disc structures, Fused Rim Lichen's reproductive bodies appear to merge together.
